\chapter{Numbers One to Ten}
\label{ch:la-numbers-one-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to ten in Latin and say why September sits in the ninth month.}

Count ūnus to decem aloud, then read the Roman tally VI-X and place September against Rome's March-start year.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ūnus duo trēs quattuor quīnque]{ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque — one to five}

\label{lesson:LA-C02-numbers-1-5}



\begin{quote}
You've seen these numbers before — worn down. Here they are new, before a thousand years of erosion set to work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The five}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{numeral} & \textbf{Latin} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
1 & \textbf{I} & \textbf{ūnus} & \emph{OO-nus} \\
2 & \textbf{II} & \textbf{duo} & \emph{DOO-oh} \\
3 & \textbf{III} & \textbf{trēs} & \emph{trayss} \\
4 & \textbf{IV} & \textbf{quattuor} & \emph{KWAT-twor} \\
5 & \textbf{V} & \textbf{quīnque} & \emph{KWEEN-kwe} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The Roman numerals \textbf{I II III IV V} are the tally you already half-know from clock faces — one, two, three strokes, then \textbf{IV} (one \emph{before} five) and \textbf{V} (five itself). (The \textbf{qu} in \emph{quattuor}/\emph{quīnque} is said \textbf{kw}, and every Latin \textbf{v} is a \textbf{w} — so \emph{quīnque} is \emph{KWEEN-kwe}.)

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin is the well the Romance tracks keep drawing from. Line these up against their descendants and you see the erosion happen:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{$\to$ French} & \textbf{$\to$ Spanish} \\
\midrule
\emph{ūnus} & un & uno \\
\emph{duo} & deux & dos \\
\emph{trēs} & trois & tres \\
\textbf{quattuor} & \textbf{quatre} & \textbf{cuatro} \\
\emph{quīnque} & cinq & cinco \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

(A purist's note: French \emph{deux} and Spanish \emph{dos} actually descend from the \textbf{accusative} \emph{duōs}, not the \emph{duo} shown — as Romance words generally do.)

\emph{Quattuor $\to$ quatre $\to$ cuatro} is the same wearing-down Hindi shows in \emph{catvāri $\to$ chār} — two branches of one ancient word (\textbf{PIE *k\textsuperscript{w}etwóres}), one softening in Europe, one in India. And they seed English too: \emph{ūnus} in \emph{unit} and \emph{union}, \emph{duo} in \emph{duo} and \emph{dual}, \emph{trēs} in \emph{trio} and \emph{triple}, \emph{quīnque} in \emph{quintet}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: A grammar seed: the first three bend}]
Here's something Latin does that its children mostly dropped: \textbf{one, two and three change their endings} to match what they count — \emph{ūnus/ūna/ūnum}, \emph{duo/duae}, \emph{trēs/tria} — while \textbf{four and up stay fixed}. You don't need the full tables yet; just notice that \emph{ūnus} is really \emph{ūn-} with a changeable tail, and file away that Latin makes even its numbers agree.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque\textquotedblright{} — remember v = w, qu = kw
  \item the erosion — \textquotedblleft{}quattuor $\to$ quatre $\to$ cuatro\textquotedblright{}
  \item the tally — I, II, III, IV, V
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to five in Latin. (\emph{Ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque}.) Which Latin word is the source of both French \emph{quatre} and Spanish \emph{cuatro}? (\textbf{quattuor}.) How is the \textbf{qu} in \emph{quīnque} pronounced? (\textbf{kw} — \emph{KWEEN-kwe}.) Which of the first five numbers \textbf{change their endings} to match what they count? (\textbf{One, two, three} — four and up stay fixed.) Next: six to ten, and the numbers hiding in the calendar.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sex septem octō novem decem]{sex, septem, octō, novem, decem — six to ten}

\label{lesson:LA-C02-numbers-6-10}



\begin{quote}
Four of these five are hiding in your calendar right now — with the wrong numbers on them. Here's why.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The five}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{numeral} & \textbf{Latin} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
6 & \textbf{VI} & \textbf{sex} & \emph{sex} \\
7 & \textbf{VII} & \textbf{septem} & \emph{SEP-tem} \\
8 & \textbf{VIII} & \textbf{octō} & \emph{OK-toh} \\
9 & \textbf{IX} & \textbf{novem} & \emph{NO-wem} \\
10 & \textbf{X} & \textbf{decem} & \emph{DEK-em} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The numerals climb by adding to five — \textbf{VI VII VIII} (five-and-one, -two, -three) — then \textbf{IX} (one \emph{before} ten) and \textbf{X}. (Remember \emph{v} = \emph{w}, so \emph{novem} is \emph{NO-wem}; and \emph{c} is always hard \emph{k}, so \emph{decem} is \emph{DEK-em}.)

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The numbers frozen in the calendar}
Say the last four out loud and read the months beside them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{month} & \textbf{but it's month \#} \\
\midrule
\emph{septem} (7) & \textbf{September} & 9 \\
\emph{octō} (8) & \textbf{October} & 10 \\
\emph{novem} (9) & \textbf{November} & 11 \\
\emph{decem} (10) & \textbf{December} & 12 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{September} literally means \textquotedblleft{}the seventh.\textquotedblright{} It sits in ninth place because the old Roman year \textbf{began in March} — so month one was March, and the seventh month was our September. When January and February were later pushed to the front, the names never moved. Every year you write four Latin numbers, each two places off, because Rome renumbered the calendar and forgot to rename the months.

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sex} $\to$ \textbf{sextet}, \textbf{sextant} (and \emph{sex-} \textquotedblleft{}six\textquotedblright{} in \emph{sexagesimal}, base-60)
  \item \emph{octō} $\to$ \textbf{octave}, \textbf{October} — while its Greek twin \emph{okt\'{\={o}}} gives \textbf{octagon} and \textbf{octopus} (eight arms)
  \item \emph{decem} $\to$ \textbf{decimal}, and — via \emph{duodecim} \textquotedblleft{}twelve\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{dozen} (its Greek cousin \emph{dekás} \textquotedblleft{}group of ten\textquotedblright{} adds \textbf{decade})
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sex, septem, octō, novem, decem\textquotedblright{} — v = w, c = k
  \item the calendar — \textquotedblleft{}septem $\to$ September, the seventh month… now ninth\textquotedblright{}
  \item the tally — VI, VII, VIII, IX, X
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count six to ten in Latin. (\emph{Sex, septem, octō, novem, decem}.) Why does \textbf{September} (\textquotedblleft{}the seventh\textquotedblright{}) fall in the ninth month? (Rome's year began in \textbf{March}; two months were later added at the front and the names never changed.) How is \emph{novem} said, and why? (\emph{NO-wem} — Latin \textbf{v} is a \textbf{w}.) What everyday base-ten word comes straight from \emph{decem}? (\textbf{decimal}.) You can now count to ten in the language every Romance number came from.
\end{tcolorbox}
